subject: Biology
title: Photosynthesis and Climate
description: Learn Photosynthesis and Climate in one minute.

hook.text: Plants absorb about 120 billion tons of carbon from the atmosphere each year.

buildup.text: Forests, grasslands, and ocean algae are massive carbon sinks, slowing climate change.

discovery.text: Rising CO₂ levels initially boost plant growth—a temporary effect called CO₂ fertilization.

twist.text: But heat stress, drought, and nutrient limits cancel out the gains. Plants can't save us alone.

climax.text: Protecting and restoring forests is one of the most effective climate strategies available.

punchline.text: Plants are Earth's lungs. They need protection.

quiz.question: What is CO₂ fertilization?
options: Higher CO₂ temporarily boosting plant growth

details.summary: Photosynthesis is Earth's primary carbon sink, with plants and algae absorbing about 120 gigatons of CO2 annually. Rising CO2 levels can fertilize plant growth but this effect is limited by water, nutrients, and temperature, and cannot offset the 36 gigatons humans emit from fossil fuels.
details.whyItMatters: Photosynthesis moderates climate change by absorbing CO2, but its capacity is limited. Understanding these limits prevents overreliance on natural carbon sinks as a climate solution and highlights the need for emission reductions.
takeaways: Land plants absorb about 30 percent of human CO2 emissions annually
CO2 fertilization increases growth but is limited by water and nutrient availability
Tropical forests are the largest terrestrial carbon sink through photosynthesis

faq.question: Can planting trees solve climate change?
faq.answer: Planting trees helps but cannot solve the problem alone. Forests absorb CO2 but cannot keep up with human emissions. Trees take decades to mature, can be destroyed by fire, and require vast land. Reducing fossil fuel emissions must be the primary strategy.

faq.question: Does more CO2 always mean more plant growth?
faq.answer: Not indefinitely. CO2 fertilization boosts growth initially, but plants also need water, nitrogen, phosphorus, and appropriate temperatures. In many regions, these co-limitations cap the CO2 benefit. Heat and drought from climate change can negate any fertilization gain.
